title: US Inflation Surges to 4.2% — The Energy Shock Behind the Numbers
summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' May 2026 Consumer Price Index report, released on 10 June, showed annual inflation accelerating to 4.2% — the highest reading in over three years. The headline figure obscures a critical distinction: the surge is almost entirely driven by energy costs tied to the Iran conflict, while underlying domestic price pressures remain comparatively subdued. Understanding that difference matters enormously for what comes next in monetary policy.
context:
- Energy prices rose 3.9% in May alone and are up 23.5% year-on-year, with petrol prices 40.5% higher than a year ago. Energy accounted for over 60% of the monthly CPI increase, meaning this is structurally an energy crisis, not broad demand overheating.

- Core CPI — excluding food and energy — rose just 0.2% on the month and 2.9% annually, indicating the domestic economy has not entered a wage-price spiral. The inflation surge remains concentrated in the externally driven energy component.

- The 4.2% reading reverses an 18-month disinflationary trend that had brought US inflation close to the Fed's 2% target. Policymakers who expected to cut rates in 2026 now face an unwanted supply-side setback that conventional monetary tools cannot directly fix.

- Supply-side oil shocks can prove transitory if the underlying conflict resolves — but the 1973 and 1979 energy crises both produced prolonged inflation precisely because elevated prices persisted long enough to change corporate and consumer behaviour, embedding expectations and triggering second-round effects.

- The key distinction for central banks is that raising interest rates can cool excess demand, but cannot produce more oil. The Fed faces an unusually difficult task: signalling that it takes inflation seriously without over-tightening an economy that is not experiencing demand-driven overheating.

title: ECB Raises Rates for First Time Since 2023, Exposing Europe's Stagflation Dilemma
summary: The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% on 11 June 2026, reversing the easing cycle it had been running since late 2023. The decision lays bare one of the most awkward challenges in central banking: what to do when inflation rises because of an external energy shock rather than domestic overheating — particularly when growth is already fragile.
context:
- The ECB had been cutting rates throughout 2024 and 2025, responding to weak eurozone growth and declining inflation. The June 2026 hike marks a sharp reversal — a central bank caught mid-easing cycle by a geopolitical supply shock entirely outside its control.

- Europe is structurally more exposed to Middle East energy disruption than the United States. The continent imports heavily from Gulf producers and has few domestic production alternatives, meaning it is more directly hurt when those supply routes are disrupted.

- This is Europe's second major energy supply shock in four years. The 2022 Russia-Ukraine war forced an emergency pivot away from Russian gas; the 2026 Iran conflict has now hit oil and liquefied natural gas supply from a different but equally critical direction.

- The ECB's revised forecasts capture the stagflation bind: eurozone inflation is now projected at 3.0% for 2026, while GDP growth has been cut to just 0.8%. Raising rates in this environment risks choking off growth without addressing the supply-side cause of inflation — the textbook definition of a stagflation trap.

- The governing council drew explicitly on the 1970s lesson that allowing energy-shock inflation to become entrenched in expectations is more damaging long-term than the short-run pain of tightening. For European businesses and households already under pressure from elevated energy bills, higher borrowing costs will compound those burdens.

title: Kevin Warsh's Fed: What the New Chair Signals for Monetary Policy
summary: As the Federal Reserve prepared for its first policy meeting under new chairman Kevin Warsh, markets turned their attention beyond the immediate rate decision to a more fundamental question: how the world's most powerful central bank will communicate, operate, and exercise its independence under new leadership. Warsh's appointment marks a significant shift in institutional philosophy, with wide-ranging implications for market volatility, the credibility of the inflation target, and the Fed's relationship with the White House.
context:
- Kevin Warsh, a former Fed governor who served from 2006 to 2011, has long been a critic of the post-2008 monetary policy orthodoxy. He has argued against quantitative easing as a structural tool and against forward guidance — the pre-announcement of future rate paths — which became central to how the Powell-era Fed managed market expectations.

- The abandonment of forward guidance is the most consequential near-term change. Under Powell, markets had come to rely on clear signals about the likely direction of rates months in advance; Warsh views pre-commitment as a constraint on the Fed's flexibility. Greater policy uncertainty translates directly into higher term premiums and increased volatility in bond and rate markets.

- Warsh's appointment by President Trump — who clashed repeatedly with Powell over the pace of rate cuts — raises questions about the de facto independence of the central bank, even if its formal statutory independence is unchanged. A Fed perceived as more politically responsive would see its inflation-fighting credibility eroded, with lasting consequences for long-term yield expectations.

- The Iran war has handed Warsh an immediate test of his stated philosophy that price stability is non-negotiable regardless of the source of inflation. His initial response — holding rates steady but removing forward guidance language suggesting cuts, and leaving a hike explicitly on the table — is consistent with that hard line on the 2% target.

- The Fed's credibility ultimately rests on the unconditional nature of its inflation mandate. If markets begin to doubt that commitment — whether because of political pressure, tolerance for supply-driven inflation, or opaque communication — the consequence would be persistently higher long-term interest rates that constrain investment and growth well beyond any individual rate decision.
